text: Section 1 states that the Information Technology Act, 2000 extends to the whole of India and, subject to the Act, also applies to certain offences or contraventions committed outside India.

Section 2 defines an intermediary to include telecom service providers, network service providers, internet service providers, web-hosting service providers, search engines, online payment sites, online-auction sites, online marketplaces and cyber cafes.
Section 2 defines a computer resource to include a computer, computer system, computer network, data, computer database or software.
Section 3 permits a subscriber to authenticate an electronic record by affixing a digital signature.
Section 3A allows authentication by a reliable electronic signature or electronic authentication technique specified in the Second Schedule.
Section 4 gives legal recognition to electronic records when statutory writing requirements are satisfied through accessible electronic form.
Section 5 gives legal recognition to electronic signatures where a law requires a signature or authentication.
Section 6 permits prescribed electronic forms for specified filings, licences, approvals, receipts and payments involving government agencies.
Section 7 permits statutory retention requirements to be satisfied by retaining records electronically when the stated conditions are met.
Section 7A applies audit provisions to documents, records or information processed and maintained in electronic form.
Section 8 recognizes publication in an Electronic Gazette where a law requires publication in the Official Gazette.
Section 10A states that a contract is not unenforceable solely because proposals, acceptances or revocations were expressed electronically.
Section 11 specifies circumstances in which an electronic record is attributed to the originator.
Section 12 provides methods by which an acknowledgment of receipt of an electronic record may be given.
Section 13 provides rules for determining the time and place of dispatch and receipt of an electronic record.
Section 14 provides that an electronic record to which a security procedure has been applied can be deemed a secure electronic record.
Section 15 sets conditions under which an electronic signature is deemed to be secure.
Section 17 permits the Central Government to appoint a Controller of Certifying Authorities.
Section 18 lists functions of the Controller including supervision of Certifying Authorities and certification of their public keys.
Section 19 permits recognition of a foreign Certifying Authority subject to the statutory conditions.
Section 21 permits a person to apply for a licence to issue electronic signature certificates.
Section 22 specifies documents and fees accompanying an application for a Certifying Authority licence.
Section 25 permits revocation of a Certifying Authority licence on specified grounds after a reasonable opportunity to show cause.
Section 26 requires notice of suspension or revocation of a Certifying Authority licence to be published in the Controller's database.
Section 28 authorizes the Controller or an authorized officer to investigate contraventions of the Act and its rules or regulations.
Section 30 requires every Certifying Authority to use secure hardware, software and procedures and maintain specified reliability and security.
Section 34 requires a Certifying Authority to disclose its electronic signature certificate and specified related information.
Section 35 permits a person to apply to a Certifying Authority for an electronic signature certificate.
Section 37 permits suspension of a Digital Signature Certificate in specified circumstances, including a subscriber request or public interest.
Section 38 permits revocation of a Digital Signature Certificate in specified circumstances.
Section 42 requires a subscriber to exercise reasonable care to retain control of the private key corresponding to the public key in the certificate.
Section 43 makes specified unauthorized acts involving computer resources liable for damages by way of compensation.
Section 43A provides compensation liability where a body corporate's negligence in reasonable security practices for sensitive personal data causes wrongful loss or gain.
Section 44 provides penalties for specified failures to furnish documents, returns or reports, file information, or maintain books and records.
Section 45 provides a residuary compensation or penalty where no separate penalty is provided for a contravention of rules or regulations.
Section 46 provides for appointment and jurisdiction of adjudicating officers for specified claims and contraventions.
Section 47 lists unfair advantage, loss caused and repetitive default as factors for adjudging compensation.
Section 48 identifies the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal as the Appellate Tribunal for purposes of the Act.
Section 57 permits an aggrieved person to appeal an order of the Controller or adjudicating officer to the Appellate Tribunal, subject to the Act.
Section 58 states that the Appellate Tribunal is guided by natural justice and is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure procedure.
Section 60 provides for application of the Limitation Act, 1963 to appeals to the Appellate Tribunal, as far as may be.
Section 62 permits an appeal from the Appellate Tribunal to the High Court within the period specified in the section.
Section 63 permits specified contraventions to be compounded subject to statutory conditions.
Section 65 punishes knowingly or intentionally concealing, destroying or altering computer source code required to be maintained by law.
Section 66 punishes dishonestly or fraudulently doing an act referred to in Section 43.
Section 66B punishes dishonestly receiving or retaining a stolen computer resource or communication device while knowing or having reason to believe it is stolen.
Section 66C punishes fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's electronic signature, password or unique identification feature.
Section 66D punishes cheating by personation through a communication device or computer resource.
Section 66E punishes specified intentional or knowing capture, publication or transmission of an image of a person's private area without consent.
Section 66F defines cyber terrorism and provides imprisonment that may extend to life imprisonment for the offence.
Section 67 punishes publication or transmission of specified obscene material in electronic form.
Section 67A punishes publication or transmission of material containing sexually explicit acts or conduct in electronic form.
Section 67B covers publication or transmission of material depicting children in sexually explicit acts and other listed activities involving such material.
Section 67C requires intermediaries to preserve and retain specified information for the prescribed duration and in the prescribed manner and format.
Section 69 permits specified government authorities to direct interception, monitoring or decryption of information through a computer resource when statutory conditions are satisfied.
Section 69A permits specified government authorities to direct blocking of public access to information through a computer resource when statutory conditions are satisfied.
Section 69B permits the Central Government to authorize a government agency to monitor and collect traffic data or information for cyber security purposes.
Section 70 permits the appropriate Government to declare a computer resource affecting Critical Information Infrastructure to be a protected system.
Section 70A permits the Central Government to designate a government organization as the national nodal agency for Critical Information Infrastructure Protection.
Section 70B establishes the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team as the national agency for incident response in cyber security.
Rule 2 defines a child as a person below eighteen years of age.
Rule 2 defines digital media as digitized content transmitted over the internet or computer networks and processed by an intermediary or specified publisher.
Rule 2 defines a social media intermediary as an intermediary that primarily or solely enables online interaction between two or more users and permits specified information activities.

Rule 2 defines synthetically generated information as specified audio, visual or audio-visual information artificially or algorithmically created, generated, modified or altered using a computer resource so that it appears real, authentic or true.
Rule 3 requires intermediaries, including specified social media and online gaming intermediaries, to observe due diligence.
Rule 3 requires an intermediary to prominently publish its rules and regulations, privacy policy and user agreement.

Rule 3 requires an intermediary to make reasonable efforts concerning users' hosting, displaying, uploading, modifying, publishing, transmitting, storing, updating or sharing of specified information.
Rule 3 requires an intermediary to inform users at least once every three months of specified consequences of non-compliance.
Rule 3 contains additional user-information obligations for intermediaries that facilitate creation or dissemination of synthetically generated information.
Rule 9 requires publishers referred to in Rule 8 to observe and adhere to the Code of Ethics.
Rule 10 requires acknowledgment of a publisher grievance within twenty-four hours and a decision within fifteen days.
Rule 11 establishes the publisher as Level I of the self-regulating mechanism.
Rule 11 requires a publisher to establish a grievance redressal mechanism and appoint a Grievance Officer based in India.
Rule 12 provides for one or more independent self-regulatory bodies of publishers.
Rule 13 establishes the Central Government Oversight Mechanism as Level III for publishers.
Rule 14 provides for an Inter-Departmental Committee to hear specified complaints concerning violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics.
Rule 15 states that a direction may concern specific content or an enumerated list and shall not require an entity to cease its operations.
Rule 16 permits an interim blocking direction without an opportunity of hearing in an emergency, subject to the rule's conditions.
Rule 17 requires the Review Committee to meet at least once every two months to review blocking directions.
Rule 19 requires publishers, subject to applicable law, to preserve records of content transmitted by them for a minimum of sixty days.
Section 43 provides only criminal imprisonment and no compensation remedy.
Section 66B punishes publication of obscene electronic material.
Section 66C specifically punishes cyber terrorism.
Section 66D carries a maximum imprisonment of ten years.
Section 69A authorizes interception, monitoring and decryption of information.
Section 69B is the provision that authorizes blocking public access to information.
Section 70A establishes CERT-In as the national agency for cyber incident response.
Section 78 requires a Deputy Superintendent of Police or higher rank to investigate offences under the Act.
Section 79 provides absolute immunity for all third-party information regardless of due diligence.
Rule 10 gives publishers thirty days to decide every grievance.
Rule 11 places publishers at Level III of the self-regulating mechanism.
Rule 15 permits a direction requiring an entity to cease its operations.
Rule 16 requires an opportunity of hearing before every emergency interim blocking direction.
Rule 17 requires the Review Committee to meet every week.
Rule 19 requires publishers to preserve transmitted content records for a maximum of thirty days.
The Information Technology Act, 2000 has reduced cybercrime in India by fifty percent since enactment.
Section 43A has been successfully used in hundreds of Indian court cases involving data breaches.
Every Indian intermediary currently complies fully with Rule 3.
The 2026 amendments to the Intermediary Rules will definitely eliminate deepfakes from Indian social media.
The Information Technology Act is the most effective cyber law in the world.
Section 79 is interpreted identically by every Indian court.
The Intermediary Rules guarantee that every age classification assigned to online curated content is correct.
Compliance with the Intermediary Rules automatically guarantees safe-harbour protection in every case.
The Information Technology Act is the only law applicable to electronic records in India.
The Rules have eliminated unlawful synthetically generated information from all online platforms in India.
